subject: effects of adjusting hyperparameters in CAR model

messages.author: 3314d7ad28eab19e
messages.subject: effects of adjusting hyperparameters in CAR model
parts:
Dear Group,

I am interested in the specification of hyperparameters for the binomial CAR model. My model is the following:

# Model with no spatial effect
form1 <- DWR ~ Snow + Hemlock + Cedar + Elevation + Slope + South + Mixed + Edge +
    Road + Impervious + Stream + Conifer + Maple + Aspen
m1<-inla(formula=form, data=ddat1, family="binomial", 
    control.compute=list(waic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE),
    control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, link=link),
    control.fixed=list(prec.intercept=0.001))

# Model with spatial effect
library(maptools)
ddat1.shp<-readShapePoly("C:\\Shawn\\MyData\\dwc_lattice.shp")
temp<-poly2nb(ddat1.shp)
adj<-nb2mat(temp, style="B", zero.policy=TRUE)
adj<-as(adj, "dgTMatrix")
ddat1.shp$idx<-1:nrow(ddat1.shp)
ddat1$idx<-ddat1.shp$idx

form1.test<-update(form1, ~ .  + f(idx, model="besag", graph=adj))
m1.test<-inla(formula=form1.test, data=ddat1, family="binomial", 
                  control.compute=list(waic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE),
                  control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, link=link),
                  control.fixed=list(prec.intercept=0.001),
                  verbose=FALSE)

The model 'm1.test' seems to effectively model spatial dependence, as indicated by a plot of Moran's I on the 'residuals' (observed - mean of predicted models). However, I am concerned about how the degree of spatial smoothing. I have been following recommendations by Beguin et al. 2012 'Hierarchical Analysis of Spatially Autocorrelated Ecological Data using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation.' The suggested rule of thumb is that the ratio between sample size and # of effective parameters should be > 20. 

In my model (m1.test), accepting default values for hyperparameters results in a model that is "overfitted" such that the ratio is 12.33. I have tried to make adjustments using code from Beguin et al., for example by including

# Adjust hyperparameters for spatial random effect
hyperpar_CAR = list(initial = -1, param=c(24.47, 0.001))
form1.test<-update(form1, ~ .  + f(idx, model="besag", graph=adj, hyper=list(theta=hyperpar_CAR)))

I have tried adjusting the values for both initial and param in 'hyperpar_CAR', but am unable to reduce the amount of smoothing to limit the number of effective parameters such that the ratio is > 20. In my case, the results seem to be more sensitive to changes in 'initial' than in 'param.' So my question is, what exactly is going on when we tweak these parameters? Especially, e.g. why is the default for 'initial' = 4, and what influence does changing 'initial' have on estimation of the spatial structure?

Apologies for the length of this question, but I thought it necessary to include more detail rather than less. 

Thanks so much for considering my question,
Shawn

messages.author: bbb9357156c132fe
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] effects of adjusting hyperparameters in CAR model
parts:
Hi Shawn,

As with all rules of thumb, the >20 is a suggestion rather than a prescription, so I wouldn't worry too much about missing it.  The number of effective parameters is a little bit of a "magical" quantity that comes from the definition of the DIC and is an indication of model complexity, but isn't a perfect one.  You didn't actually say what the expected number of parameters or the sample size is, but as long as it's not alarming, things are usually ok.  It would also be useful to know what Ntrials is.  This problem is better behaved if there is more than one experiment per region.

A couple of little things.  

The first is that the scale.model=TRUE option in the f() call would be useful (see this tutorial here http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/tutorials/inla/scale.model/scale-model-tutorial.pdf).  This should make it easier to set the priors. 

The second thing is that to reduce the number of effective parameters, you need *more* smoothing, not less.  This is because if there is "infinite" smoothing, the Besag model looks just like a completely flat surface, which only needs one parameter to describe it

The "initial" parameter tells the optimiser where to start looking for the mode. In theory there shouldn't be huge dependence on this, but in practice, if it's set to a "weird" value, you will see it.  For example "initial=4" says that INLA will start looking for the value of the smoothing paramteter at exp(4) [things are internally on the log-scale].  If the model is correctly scaled (see the tutorial), then this would correspond to a standard deviation of around 0.2.  So changing initial to -1 with that prior will have INLA begin looking at the log-smoothing parameters at values around -1, while the prior is tightly concentrated at values around 10.  This may explain the bad numerical behaviour that you are seeing.

Hope this helps

Best wishes,

Dan

messages.author: 3314d7ad28eab19e
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] effects of adjusting hyperparameters in CAR model
parts:
Hi Dan,

Very useful clarification. To follow up, I have a irregular grid with 9,362 cells (2 km x 2 km) in which presence/absence of deer has been recorded. Surveys were rather crude so unfortunately I am restricted to using a 0/1 response at the cell level. Using default values for the prior, the number of effective parameters were 758.62. Changing initial to -1 yielded 584 effective parameters. 

Thank you for the tutorial, I will look into that.

I have a more general question for this problem, which seems broadly applicable. I am somewhat interested in model predictive accuracy (which increases with model complexity), but perhaps more so in the estimation of fixed effects. I have approached this problem using INLA because I want to account for residual spatial autocorrelation, such that I can have confidence in coefficient estimates and the variability around those estimates. For this objective, how concerned should one be about model complexity? For example, if I use an uninformative prior, it seems that model complexity is greater. Would this have any negative effect on fixed effects estimates, as opposed to specifying an informative prior for more spatial smoothing?

This is my first attempt at applying Bayesian methods to this problem, so thanks again for your interest & patience. 
best,
Shawn
